::: {#sol-lstm-pixels}

```{python}
#| code-fold: show
pixel_lstm = make_reader(nn.LSTM, 1)
lstm_norms = train(pixel_lstm, n_epochs=20)
lstm_acc = accuracy(pixel_lstm)
print(lstm_acc, max(lstm_norms))
# The prose below says the LSTM does better; stop the render if it does not.
assert lstm_acc > max(clipped_acc, pixel_acc)
```

Yes.
The [LSTM](https://morrison-lab.github.io/lds/chapters/cnn-rnn.html#def-lstm) classifies `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * py$lstm_acc)` of the test digits correctly,
against `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * py$clipped_acc)` for the clipped pixel reader.
Its cell state $\vecf{c}_t$ changes only by the [gates'](https://morrison-lab.github.io/lds/chapters/cnn-rnn.html#def-gate) products and sums,
with no squashing activation between one step and the next.
So a [gradient](https://morrison-lab.github.io/lds/chapters/linear-regression.html#def-gradient) can pass back along it through many steps
when the forget gate stays near 1 [@goodfellow2016deep, section 10.10.1].
Its largest gradient [norm](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/linear-algebra-inner-products.html#def-norm) during training was `r sprintf("%.1f", max(unlist(py$lstm_norms)))`,
against `r sprintf("%.0f", py$max_norm_seen)` for the pixel reader of @sol-pixels.

:::
